body: The tables have been pushed back and the last of the food is still out, and at the far end of the afternoon a man of eighty is telling the one about the flood in 1954. He has told it before. A boy of about eleven, sitting on a stacking chair with a paper plate on his knees, says the line about the piano a beat before the old man gets to it, and nobody tells him off, because that is where the line goes and he has done it correctly. A woman near the urn says the road was Chapel Street, not Chapel Road. The man says Chapel Street, then, and carries on from where he was.
Three people told that story. One of them said most of the words. What was going on in the hall was not a performance in front of an audience but a thing being held jointly, with checks.
The assumption underneath nearly all Western thinking about this is that oral tradition is what people had before writing — a lossy, approximate stage that literacy arrives and replaces.

The assumption does not survive much scrutiny. Oral traditions are frequently more accurate across long periods than anybody expects, because they are built for it: metre, rhyme, formula, fixed phrases arriving in a fixed order, a shape in which a wrong word audibly does not fit. And it is worth taking the word keep literally, because English has two different verbs hiding inside it. A text is stored. A story is kept, in the sense that a promise is kept or a garden is kept — an activity, performed by somebody, which stops the moment the somebody stops. The hall did not contain a copy of the flood story. It contained the people who were keeping it.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations, 46 of them on air today. Two of the numbers, HM 367.20 and HM 367.50, are assigned to Story Hour and to Inspire Stories. Both are in build, not yet on air, still silent.

Holding frequencies for telling rather than for music is an awkward commitment on a band whose obvious business is songs. Spoken material is slower to make, harder to schedule and far easier to skip, and no version of it fills an hour as efficiently as an hour of worship does. It is worth the trouble because of what the format does that a page cannot. A written text survives without anybody caring about it. A spoken one only survives inside a community that is still telling it, which is a stricter test, and a band that only ever sang would be keeping half of what it was given.

The stricter test is not the only difference. A story that is told carries information no transcript of it holds: who is entitled to tell it and who is not, whom it may be told to, at what time of year, at what point in an evening, and what the room is meant to be doing while it goes on. None of that is on the page. There are archives full of stories collected carefully by people who meant well, and what sits in them is the words with the instructions deleted. It is the difference between a recipe and a kitchen.

Scripture spent a long time as both and shows it. Whole tracts of it are shaped for the mouth rather than the eye: lines that say the same thing twice in different words so a listener gets a second chance at it, refrains that come round, structures that fold back so the middle is the point. It reads better aloud than silently, and that is no accident. The Shema itself is an instruction about speaking — teach them to your children, talk of them when you sit in your house and when you walk by the way, when you lie down and when you rise up. Not file them. Talk of them.
So the two are not a worse technology and a better one. They are two ways of keeping a thing, and they fail differently, which is the part worth attending to.

The obvious answer to fragility is to write it down. Record it, archive it, get it safe. That deserves a fair hearing, because writing has saved an enormous amount, and much of what is known about peoples who no longer exist is known only because somebody sat down and took it out of the air. But look at what the durability consists of. A written text survives indifference. It sits on a shelf through two centuries of nobody wanting it and is still legible when somebody finally does. That is a real strength and it carries a hidden cost, because a thing that requires nobody tends to get nobody.
Writing is the technology that lets everybody off.

A woman is driving her two children back from a hospital visit, an hour and a bit of dual carriageway in the dark, and the younger one asks for the one about the bees. She has not thought about it in years. She starts it anyway, and four lines in she hears her mother’s phrasing come out of her own mouth, including the pause before the last line, which she had always taken for her mother being funny and now understands is where the story needs it. Her son corrects her once, on a name. He has it from the same place she does. She has never read the story anywhere. There is nowhere to read it.
Nothing in that was retrieved from anything. It was in her, in the specific shape it had been given to her, including a pause she could not have explained.

Oral transmission does fail, and when it fails it fails completely. One generation that does not bother and the thing is gone, with no shelf to go back to and no way of finding out what was in it. It drifts as well. A name shifts, a detail is improved by somebody with a better ear for a story than a memory for the facts, and none of it can be audited, because the only record of what it used to be is the same set of mouths that changed it.

But the fragility is doing something, and it is worth seeing what. A thing that can only be kept by being said has to be said, and so it recruits people. It needs a teller, and a room, and somebody young enough to still be there in fifty years, and it collapses without them. That requirement is not a weakness writing came along and fixed. It is the mechanism by which a story stays attached to a living community rather than to a building with opening hours. The text on the shelf asks nothing of anybody, and gets exactly that.

So oral tradition is not a primitive stage before literacy. It is a different technology with different strengths and a much harder failure mode, and its central strength is the one nobody counts: it cannot be kept by accident. Every generation that has it has it because somebody older opened their mouth in a hall, or on a car journey, or at the end of a meal, and somebody younger was close enough to hear it and to correct it later.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing, so here is the part that is not.

The band carries four kinds of programming. There is music, which is most of it. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, safe to have on with children in the room. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. The storytelling numbers named above are assigned and in build, not yet on air, which leaves the question of where the telling is actually happening today, and the answer is not where most adults would look for it.

Put on HM 361.90 — Jubilee Kids Party. It is a children’s praise station and grown-ups skip past it, which is a mistake if any of the above has landed, because children are where oral transmission has always lived. The material is built the way kept things are built: short, repeated without apology, call-and-response, the same handful of songs coming round again so that a five-year-old has them by heart without anybody having taught a lesson. And a child is the strictest checker in the business. Get a word wrong in the second verse and you will be corrected at volume, in the car, by somebody who cannot read. That is the flood story in the hall, running on a Tuesday afternoon in your kitchen.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — it is built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. If you would like it closer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it opens like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band finds out which frequencies people are reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So put HM 361.90 on this week in the room where the children already are, and then do the part that is not automatic: learn one of them yourself. Not properly, and not all of it — enough to start it in the car with the radio off. The station will do the repetition, which is the expensive half of the job. The half a broadcast cannot do is a mouth in the room, and that has to be somebody’s, and in most houses there is nobody else it could be.
